#5189. Best Crypto-Friendly Banks: 5 Options for Crypto Investors and Businesses

Home » Cryptopedia » Best Crypto-Friendly Banks: 5 Options for Crypto Investors and Businesses

Which banks will support your crypto habits?

Finding a crypto-friendly bank in 2026 is not as simple as opening an account with a traditional financial institution. Some banks allow transfers to cryptocurrency exchanges like Coinbase, while others offer built-in crypto trading, digital asset custody, or specialized banking services for Web3 businesses.

The best option depends on where you live, whether you are an individual investor or a crypto business, and which digital asset services you need. Some providers also impose restrictions on specific exchanges, transaction limits, or crypto-related business activities.

In this guide, we compare crypto-friendly banks and fintech providers, examining their supported services, availability, fees, and limitations to help you find the right banking solution in 2026.

A crypto-friendly bank makes it easier for individuals and businesses to interact with the cryptocurrency market through traditional financial services. Depending on the provider, this may include allowing transfers to and from crypto exchanges, offering crypto trading or payment features, or providing banking services to eligible crypto companies.

Not all crypto-friendly providers offer the same features. Some let customers buy, sell, and hold digital assets directly, while others simply support transfers to selected platforms like Kraken or provide financial services to Web3 businesses. Some are licensed banks, while others are fintech companies that partner with banks to deliver their services.

Before exploring the best crypto-friendly banks, consider the main advantages and potential drawbacks.

If you’re looking for the best crypto-friendly bank to join in 2023, you’re in the right place! This list breaks down some of the top banks for cryptocurrency from a variety of fields, including traditional banking, business banking, and personal accounts.

Revolut remains one of the more accessible options for people who want to manage traditional money and cryptocurrency through a single financial app.

Revolut is a digital banking platform that combines traditional financial services with cryptocurrency features. In supported markets, customers can use its app to buy, sell, hold, and transfer cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum. Available assets and features depend on the customer’s country and account eligibility.

Revolut also supports crypto withdrawals and deposits through selected external wallets and blockchain networks. However, transaction fees, supported assets, and withdrawal limits vary. Its cryptocurrency services are provided by separate legal entities from its banking services, and crypto holdings are not covered by standard bank deposit protection.

Wirex flips the script amongst the other ‘best crypto-friendly banks’ contenders. While other platforms began their story as traditional banks and slowly moved to cryptocurrency acceptance, Wirex set out to be the world’s leading crypto bank from day one.

Wirex is a global fintech platform combining traditional currencies, cryptocurrency services, and payment cards. Users in eligible markets can buy, sell, exchange, and hold supported digital assets, as well as use available payment services to spend their funds.

Wirex also hosts a cross-chain bridge, offers crypto-linked cards, and a Cryptoback rewards programme, which advertises rewards of up to 8% on eligible purchases.

Actual rewards depend on the card programme, subscription, and applicable conditions. Wirex is not a traditional bank; its services are provided through regulated entities and financial partners, depending on the customer’s location.

Mercury is a US-based financial technology company providing business banking services through partner banks. It is particularly relevant to eligible cryptocurrency and Web3 startups, DAOs, and investment funds that need traditional financial infrastructure to manage their operations.

Businesses can use Mercury to manage fiat deposits, payments, expenses, and transfers to supported cryptocurrency exchanges, including Coinbase and Gemini. However, Mercury does not hold cryptocurrencies or provide crypto trading services.

It supports most eligible US-registered businesses, including those founded by international entrepreneurs, but does not accept applications from crypto exchanges or money services businesses.

Monzo is a UK-based digital bank that allows customers to use their accounts with selected cryptocurrency exchanges.

Although it does not offer native cryptocurrency trading, customers can transfer money to supported platforms, including Coinbase, making it an option for investors who want to manage traditional banking and crypto purchases separately.

Monzo applies transaction monitoring and restrictions to cryptocurrency-related payments. For example, it currently blocks payments to Binance while allowing transfers to a range of other exchanges. Its cryptocurrency payment allowance is also limited, so customers should check the latest terms before making large transactions.

Ally Bank is a US-based digital bank offering traditional banking products, including checking accounts, savings accounts, and investment services. Unlike specialist crypto-friendly financial platforms, Ally does not provide direct cryptocurrency trading or cryptocurrency custody through its banking services.

Customers cannot transfer cryptocurrencies directly to Ally accounts, which accept transactions in US dollars. Ally Invest also does not currently support direct cryptocurrency trading, although customers can access certain crypto-related investment products, including cryptocurrency funds and publicly traded companies involved in the industry.

Ally is therefore better suited to customers looking for conventional banking and investment services rather than direct access to cryptocurrency exchanges or digital assets.

Choosing a crypto-friendly bank involves more than finding a financial institution that allows cryptocurrency transactions. The right option depends on your location, investment activities, and whether you need basic exchange transfers or more advanced crypto-related services.

Here are five important factors to consider:

Check whether the bank supports transfers to your preferred cryptocurrency exchanges, such as Coinbase, Kraken, or Binance. Some financial institutions restrict payments to specific platforms or apply additional security checks to crypto-related transactions.

Compare account maintenance fees, international transfer costs, currency conversion charges, and any limits on cryptocurrency-related payments. Some providers also charge separate fees for buying, selling, or withdrawing digital assets.

Look for providers with appropriate regulatory authorisation and transparent security policies. Check whether eligible fiat deposits are covered by a recognised deposit guarantee scheme and understand that cryptocurrency holdings generally receive different protections.

Crypto-related banking services are not available everywhere. Before opening an account, check whether the provider accepts customers in your country and whether its cryptocurrency features are accessible in your region.

If you operate a Web3 startup, blockchain company, or cryptocurrency-related business, check the provider’s business eligibility requirements. Some platforms, including Mercury, support eligible technology and Web3 companies but exclude certain activities, such as operating a cryptocurrency exchange or money services business.

Crypto-friendly banks and financial platforms make it easier to manage traditional money and cryptocurrency in one place. However, their safety depends on regulation, banking partnerships, and security measures.

An important distinction is that eligible fiat deposits may be protected by deposit guarantee schemes, while cryptocurrencies generally are not. Crypto assets also carry risks such as market volatility, custody issues, and potential losses.

Not every crypto-friendly platform is a licensed bank. Providers such as Wirex and Mercury may operate through regulated entities or partner banks. Before choosing one, check its licences, account terms, and what protections actually apply to your funds.

Several financial institutions and fintech platforms support cryptocurrency-related transactions. Revolut and Wirex offer crypto services in eligible markets, while Monzo supports transfers to selected cryptocurrency exchanges. Mercury provides banking services to eligible Web3 businesses, whereas Ally Bank primarily offers traditional banking and investment products.

The best option depends on your needs. Revolut is suitable for individuals seeking integrated crypto services, Wirex focuses on cryptocurrency payments and spending, and Mercury caters to eligible Web3 businesses. Monzo can be useful for UK customers transferring money to supported exchanges.

Yes, many banks and financial platforms allow transfers to Coinbase, although availability depends on the customer’s location, payment method, and account restrictions. Always check your bank’s current cryptocurrency payment policy and Coinbase’s supported funding methods before initiating a transfer.

Some institutions also block transactions involving specific exchanges. Customers should review their provider’s terms and conditions before making crypto-related transfers.

Eligible deposits held with licensed banks may be covered by national deposit protection schemes, depending on the institution, account type, and applicable limits. However, cryptocurrency holdings are generally not covered by traditional bank deposit insurance. Fintech platforms may also use partner banks, so customers should identify the institution actually holding their deposits and verify the applicable protection.

#5188. Web3Auth Exploit Doesn't Affect Trust Wallet: Products That Might be Affected

Crypto industry is dealing with another security turmoil, as a breach at Web3Auth, the wallet authentication infrastructure owned by Consensys, has exposed private keys of certain Keplr wallets, according to the official statement of TrustWallet representative on X.

The November 7 incident led to emergency service suspensions and recovery efforts, which could add pressure to an already fragile crypto market.

Web3Auth confirmed that a security issue in its infrastructure had compromised certain embedded wallets integrated with Keplr, especially accounts created through Google or Apple login.

Blockchain analytics firm Bitquery estimates that attackers drained at least $6 million from more than 44,000 wallets.

Those wallets sit across eight Cosmos ecosystem networks, including Cosmos Hub, Osmosis, Celestia and Injective.

Keplr warned users from depositing into compromised accounts and Web3Auth on their side suspended embedded wallet service, actively working on a recovery of vulnerable assets.

MetaMask stated that there is no evidence of affected users, though the situation is still under control. Trust Wallet has been unaffected, says its representative Felix. The impact on other third-party integrations is yet to be confirmed.

On October 29, Binance reportedly suffered a massive security breach involving around $6.3 billion, while Bitget was hit by an exploit estimated at $387.5 million in September.

Earlier in 2026, KelpDAO lost around $290 million after an exploit involving cross-chain infrastructure.

DeFi protocols, wallet infrastructures, smart contracts: those kinds of incidents are relevant for almost every project on the market. Exploits directly affect market sentiment, investors losses and safety in the industry in general.

Projects that rely on embedded wallet technology and Cosmos-related assets have unfortunately been affected directly and repeated security failures might damage their market picture state even further.

Luckily, there's no proven link between the Web3Auth expoit and declines on the market as a whole, including assets like Bitcoin and Ethereum. The investigations and rapid protocol patches are being released after more than 24 hours since the discovery.

#5187. Wall Street can stop a tokenized share, but can it stop a stock perp?

Wall Street is fighting over crypto-style stock trading as major companies reject tokenized shares and traditional exchanges challenge new derivatives markets.

Costco recently made news when it strongly objected to a blockchain version of its shares. And while the supermarket giant did raise a set of pretty valid concerns regarding the potential risks of tokenization, the problem was that traders can actually already buy a blockchain-based contract (i.e., token) that follows its stock price.

The company is among 67 issuers in OKXICE's Nov. 5 objection notice, blocking third-party tokenized versions of their stock from the proposed venue backed by the New York Stock Exchange's owner.

Meanwhile, Kalshi lists a Costco perpetual, which offers price exposure without giving its buyer any shares.

The two products show how differently finance treats owning a company and trading its price: an issuer can stop its stock tokens from trading through one blockchain arrangement, while contracts tied to that stock follow a separate legal route.

That route is now being challenged in court, with established Wall Street firms competing to offer these contracts.

Shares give shareholders an interest in a business, along with the voting and distribution rights attached to the particular class of stock they own. Putting that interest on a blockchain can change how it's transferred while preserving what its owner is entitled to receive.

OKXICE's proposed model uses a tokenization provider acting through a registered broker-dealer to hold one underlying share for each token. Each token represents an entitlement to that share, and customers would trade them against dollar-linked stablecoins in automated asset pools.

Those pools can produce different prices from conventional exchanges. The ownership claim and the price you can get for it are separate concerns.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's September exemption allows qualifying venues to operate outside ordinary exchange registration, subject to conditions.

Tokens must preserve equivalent shareholder rights, including votes, dividends, and a claim on residual assets if the company is liquidated. Any token that just copies a share price doesn't qualify.

But the underlying company also gets a say. Before offering stock tokenized by an unaffiliated third party, an exchange has to notify the issuer, and each company has 30 days from receiving its notice to object.

The SEC's staff guidance confirms that a timely objection must be disclosed and prevents the venue from offering that token under the exemption.

Costco and dozens of others have already exercised that right, with their objections applying to OKXICE, and the companies haven't collectively explained their motives. The list therefore tells us little about their views on other forms of tokenization or contracts referencing their share prices.

A Costco perp works differently. You go long to gain when the stock rises, or short to gain when it falls. The contract has no scheduled expiry, and Kalshi's stock-perps documentation says holders receive neither shares nor voting rights.

Reported trailing 24-hour notional volume from one Kalshi data snapshot retrieved Nov. 6, 2026, at 13:49 UTC, rounded to the nearest $1,000. Covers only the four stocks named in Kalshi's Nov. 3 launch announcement, not its full stock-perp market. The exact rolling-window cutoff is not separately timestamped. Turnover is not investor count, new capital, or a measure of bullish demand.

Source: Kalshi market data, retrieved Nov. 6, 2026, 13:49 UTC · Kalshi's Nov. 3 stock-perpetual launch announcement

That also means you can take substantial exposure with relatively little money. Costco's market page showed maximum leverage of 4.9 times on Nov. 6, meaning $1,000 of collateral supports $4,900 of price exposure.

A 10% move would cost $490 before fees and other adjustments, nearly half the original collateral. If collateral falls below the required minimum, the platform can close the position.

Even though the contract has no expiry, you may lose the ability to wait for a recovery.

Assumes identical percentage price moves and unchanged position size. Loss = starting exposure x price decline. Excludes fees, funding, dividends, lot-size rounding and other adjustments. Liquidation could occur before an illustrated decline, so the bars are not a path an actual position can necessarily survive. The 4.9x input is Costco's displayed maximum on Nov. 6, 2026.

Source: Kalshi Costco market: displayed maximum leverage on Nov. 6, 2026 · Kalshi stock-perp mechanics and liquidation risks; illustrative calculations by CryptoSlate

Perps also need a way to keep their price near the underlying asset. Conventional futures have an eventual settlement date, while perpetuals use recurring payments between traders, called funding, to discourage a persistent gap.

When the contract trades too high relative to its reference price, longs have to pay shorts, and when it trades too low, payments run the other way.

These funding transfers can reward taking the less popular side, but they also mean that correctly predicting a stock's direction doesn't fully determine your return.

Kalshi says cash dividends generate contractual cash adjustments for long and short positions, although those payments don't make contract holders shareholders, nor does perpetual mean permanently open.

Kalshi's Costco page lists trading from Sunday evening to Friday afternoon, Eastern time. Its documentation warns that customers cannot open or close positions during closures.

On Nov. 3, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig said equity perpetuals could begin trading on eligible exchanges registered with the derivatives regulator and notice-registered with the SEC. He described the products as deemed approved under Regulation 40.3, which permits approval when the review period expires without a notice of non-approval.

The agency treats them as security futures, placing them under a joint regulatory framework. Their lack of an expiry date is at the heart of the challenge to that classification.

The Capital Markets Alliance Association, whose court filings include declarations from Cboe and Citadel Securities, wants to stop the approvals. It argues that a contract without future delivery cannot qualify as a security future.

In an October SEC submission, Cboe argued that the contracts fall under security-based swaps, agreements that transfer financial exposure linked to securities under different rules. It also warned that stock-perp trades would escape the securities markets' consolidated surveillance system even when traders hedge them with ordinary shares.

Cboe has a commercial stake in the outcome, but its argument raises a substantive issue about which safeguards should follow a trade that tracks a stock without delivering it.

Judge Valerie Caproni's Nov. 3 order found the challengers likely to succeed in arguing that the CFTC exceeded its authority. She nevertheless denied an emergency restraining order because the alliance hadn't demonstrated the imminent, irreparable harm required for that relief.

The approvals remained undisturbed at that stage, despite the judge's preliminary assessment of the CFTC's legal position. The order set Nov. 6 for the government's opposition to a preliminary injunction and Nov. 10 for the alliance's reply.

Meanwhile, the NYSE's parent is pursuing both markets. ICE announced an investment and agreement with Trade[XYZ] on Oct. 29 to bring its Hyperliquid-based perpetual markets into the US.

The planned regulated venue still requires approvals, including for leveraged trading. ICE expects distribution to include its OKX joint venture, subject to that venture's own approvals.

The same exchange group backing tokenized shares sees an opportunity in selling exposure to their prices. The dispute is partly over which institutions can offer crypto's trading model, and which rules they must follow.

The difference for investors is what each product promises. Qualifying share tokens must preserve shareholder rights while introducing the costs and risks of their trading platform. Perps offer leveraged exposure governed by collateral requirements, funding payments, and contractual adjustments.

Costco's objection shows how an issuer can stop the first product on a particular venue, while the court challenge concerns regulators' authority to approve the second. The ticker may be familiar, but the rights and risks come from the contract you buy.

#5185. I’m Running the New York City Marathon Topless. The Reason Is Not What You Think.

It was my 18-mile long run, the farthest I'd gone so far in my New York City Marathon training, when I felt anxiety creep into my ankles. Central Park was full of life and happiness, but I was suddenly acutely aware of every mile, every ache, and every vulnerability I couldn't outrun. “I could just stop right now,” I thought.

A year earlier, I was in active treatment for breast cancer at 32. I had undergone chemotherapy, a mastectomy, and reconstruction, and was still learning to recognize my new body. Now, I was preparing to run 26.2 miles, completely topless, with my scars visible.

But I pushed through the fear: This was exactly why I chose to run in the first place. Not because I’ve overcome everything or that I have nothing left to hide—but because I’m learning to show up as I am: Uncomfortable, imperfect, and still moving forward. I’m running like this in the hopes that my story might help save another woman’s life. If seeing me and learning about my journey helps her speak up or look into her own breast cancer risk, this run becomes bigger than me.

In 2023, I left my career as an associate in wealth management at Merrill Lynch to raise my son. Six short months after I resigned, everything changed.

I found a lump. My ob-gyn told me I was too young for a mammogram. An ultrasound came back benign. It was a third doctor, a breast surgeon, who finally took me seriously and sent me for a mammogram, a biopsy, and an MRI. She saved my life.

I was leaving the gym on an ordinary Thursday when the call came. I had breast cancer in both breasts: stage 2 triple-negative cancer on one side and stage 1 ER/PR-positive cancer on the other.

The world went blurry, and every sound was muffled. Was I dying? My son was only one. I couldn't leave him without a mother, and my husband without his partner. I had so much more life to live, and so much more to do. How had the first two appointments missed this?

My husband, Elio, and I built my care team at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, and together we mapped out a plan: chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and surgeries. Each decision I made along the way helped me feel a little more in control.

One of the hardest parts of treatment was confronting how much my body had changed. When I finally had my mastectomy, I braced myself to be horrified when the bandages came off. I shed one tear. It hit me that things would never be the same and that a part of my body I'd tied to my femininity and sexuality had been changed forever. I faced a choice no woman should have to make. For me, it was this or facing my mortality.

But the moment that still gets me isn't the one in front of the mirror. It was the afternoon my then-two-year-old son caught a glimpse of my chest.

"Mommy, you have a boo boo?” He asked. “Are you hurt? Do you need to go to the hosminal?"

I had tried to protect my son from knowing what I was going through—no two-year-old should have to learn what cancer is before they learn the alphabet. But still, he could tell something was wrong. I was proud of his sympathy and awareness, but at the same time, I was heartbroken he noticed. I dreaded telling him about my cancer diagnosis—especially given my BRCA diagnosis and the unknowns about whether I had passed it along to him.

Later, changing in a gym locker room for the first time since surgery, I flinched, covering my chest as I pulled off my sports bra. I never would have done that before cancer. Was I ashamed of the scars? Nervous that I looked different? Probably a bit of both. I gave myself grace for that instinctive reaction, but also promised myself then that I would no longer let shame drive how I felt about my body. My scars are evidence that I lived. They stand for tenacity, resilience, and bravery—traits I want my son to have and how I want him to remember me.

During treatment, I set a goal to run my first half marathon a few months after my mastectomy. It kept me focused and gave me something to look forward to, something beyond appointments, medications, and the uncertainty of treatment. Crossing the finish line felt powerful. I thought of all the work that I’d put in to get there and the many training sessions where I chose to show up for myself every day.

But shortly after, I was disappointed to learn I would need to continue oral chemotherapy to help reduce the risk of recurrence. This pushed my recovery timeline back and meant I’d have to wait longer for my reconstructive surgeries. So I set another goal: if I could run 13.1 miles, I could run 26.2 the following year, when I’d be done with treatment and surgeries.

I decided I would also run topless, putting on display the very thing I vowed to never hide. No shirt, no bra. To prevent chafing and provide makeshift support, I plan on using special styling tape donated by NOOD.

I would do it for the women who might have questions they want to ask their doctors, who feel like something isn’t right but keep minimizing their concerns. And I would also do it for the other survivors out there. I hope that by seeing me run, they also feel more comfortable in their bodies, scars and all.

I set my sights on the New York City Marathon, running with Fred’s Team, Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center’s charity partner. I even created a subteam, Team Laklak, named after the beauty brand I co-founded during my cancer journey, offering science-based makeup that’s still full of color and fun. I’m proud that we’ve raised $45,000 to date for the very hospital that saved my life. It feels like such a full-circle moment that the beauty company I dreamed up while sitting in treatment chairs there can now give back to other women in this way.

I’m not the first woman to run a marathon topless, but I will be the first in New York City. In 2024, Louise Butcher also ran the London Marathon, showing off the scars from her mastectomy and flat closure reconstruction for similar reasons. I chose to reconstruct with implants—and I’m not sure if people will find my run more taboo or sexualized because of it. They shouldn’t. Louise and I faced the same disease and underwent similar treatments.

On November 1, I'll finish my 26.2 miles back in Central Park, the same park where I once thought, “I could just stop right now.”

My story is about more than learning to embrace my body after cancer. It's also about what can happen when women are dismissed, when they question their instincts, or when they assume they are too young to be at risk.

Breast cancer doesn't discriminate by age. Approximately one in eight women in the United States will be diagnosed in their lifetime, and a diagnosis can happen well before the age many women associate with routine screening. I was fortunate to find a breast surgeon who listened to me and pursued further testing, but not every woman knows what questions to ask or where to turn when something doesn't feel right. A breast cancer risk assessment tool can be a useful place to start. While it cannot diagnose cancer or replace medical advice from a physician, it can help women better understand their personal risk and discuss whether additional evaluation or screening may be appropriate.

Whether we're navigating cancer or chasing a marathon finish line, we will all have moments when we want to stop. We may not feel fearless or ready. We may not know exactly what comes next. But we can take the next step, ask the next question, and learn to trust ourselves along the way.

I'm running topless because I no longer want to hide my scars. I'm running because I'm still here and because I can. But most of all, I'm doing this in the hope that another woman will feel a little more empowered to take charge of her own story.

Lauren Spiezia is a breast cancer survivor who carries the BRCA2 mutation and the founder of Laklak Beauty, a clean cosmetic brand built from her experience as an oncology patient. More at laklakbeauty.com/run.

#5182. Bitcoin traders could mistake this Binance data change for a rush to sell

Coin Metrics’ November 4 notice complicates Binance balance signals as traders look for evidence of demand before CPI.

Bitcoin is trading near $76,000 ahead of Tuesday's US inflation report, while reported spot selling puts the strength of demand in focus. A warning from data provider Coin Metrics complicates one apparent signal: a larger reported Binance wallet balance can reflect expanded address coverage without fresh coins arriving.

Bitcoin was quoted at $75,871 on CryptoSlate's price page when captured at 10:42 UTC on Nov. 7. That puts $76,000 in view as a rounded market price, rather than an established technical support level.

CryptoSlate's Nov. 7 report cited CryptoQuant analyst Darkfost describing more aggressive spot selling than buying on Binance and Coinbase. Coin Metrics' coverage notice concerns a different measurement and does not invalidate that trading signal.

The upcoming inflation release gives traders a defined window to compare potential selling with actual demand. A balance chart alone cannot show whether holders have just moved coins onto an exchange, or sold them.

In its Nov. 4 notice, Coin Metrics said it planned to update exchange-address data after additional addresses were disclosed. It anticipated significant increases in some hourly supply metrics that day and daily metrics on Nov. 5, particularly for Binance BTC measures in native units and US dollars.

The provider said the planned changes would reflect broader address coverage without a corresponding change in actual exchange holdings. The notice supplies a reason to question an apparent jump, but it does not quantify one.

Coin Metrics' exchange-supply methodology counts balances in identified hot and cold wallets at the end of an interval. It also warns that undiscovered addresses can leave the measure below actual holdings. Identifying an additional wallet therefore changes what the dataset sees, without establishing that a customer has just deposited more Bitcoin.

Dollar-denominated supply adds another moving part: it is calculated from the coin balance and the USD price. A rise in that dollar reading alone cannot isolate an increase in the number of coins.

The next step is to examine deposits, which Coin Metrics defines as assets sent to an exchange during an interval, using addresses it identifies as exchange-owned. Those observations measure transfers. They do not establish that the transferred coins were sold.

Comparability matters here too. Coin Metrics' point-in-time documentation says standard exchange histories can be revised when new addresses are discovered. Point-in-time histories keep past values fixed, but newly discovered addresses still enter coverage from their discovery date onward. Choosing that series does not automatically make every date comparable.

Evidence of execution comes from a different dataset. Coin Metrics' trade records include time, price and amount, plus the taker's side where known. A sell taker is an incoming order that removes a resting bid. That identifies aggressive selling, rather than merely coins held at an exchange.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics calendar schedules October CPI for Tuesday, Nov. 10 at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time, or 13:30 UTC.

Inflation news could change expectations for monetary policy, with Treasury yields and appetite for risk among the possible transmission channels. The Federal Reserve's explanation describes how expected policy changes can affect longer-term rates and asset prices. These are possible channels for the coming release, rather than a prediction of Bitcoin's direction.

For this demand test, comparable flows would show whether coins are moving onto exchanges, while executed spot trades would show whether sellers are executing against standing buy orders. The price response would then help assess whether buyers are absorbing that pressure: aggressive selling alongside a resilient price would be consistent with absorption; sustained price weakness would make that reading harder to defend.

These observations need to cover comparable periods and measurements. They would not, by themselves, connect a particular depositor with a particular sale. For holders watching the inflation release, the useful signal is how actual selling meets demand, with Binance's changing wallet coverage accounted for first.
